questions.q: Which of the following even numbers CANNOT be expressed as a sum of two or more consecutive natural numbers: 18, 22, 32, 36?
questions.a: 32 cannot be expressed. 18 = 5+6+7 or 3+4+5+6; 22 = 4+5+6+7; 36 = 11+12+13 or 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8. A wrong answer (e.g., picking 18) reveals the student thinks all even numbers work or confuses the pattern with odd numbers.

questions.q: Explain why 10 can be written as a sum of consecutive numbers (1+2+3+4) but 8 cannot, even though both are even.
questions.a: 10 has an odd factor 5 (10 = 2 × 5), allowing a sum of 4 terms centered at 2.5 (1,2,3,4). 8 is a power of 2 (2³) with no odd factor >1, so no such centering is possible. A wrong answer (e.g., "8 is smaller") shows the student relies on size rather than factor structure.

questions.q: Find a sum of consecutive natural numbers that equals 44. Show your steps.
questions.a: 44 = 2 × 22 = 4 × 11. Odd factor 11 suggests 11 terms centered at 4: but 4 - 5 = -1 (invalid). Try odd factor from 44/2? Actually, 44 = 11 × 4. Use k=8 (even number of terms): sum = 8/2 × (2n+7) = 4(2n+7) = 44 → 2n+7=11 → n=2. So 2+3+4+5+6+7+8+9 = 44. A wrong answer like "11+12+13+14=50" shows incorrect centering or term count.

questions.q: Compare the number of ways to write 30 and 36 as sums of consecutive natural numbers. Which has more representations and why?
questions.a: 30 has odd factors 3,5,15 → 3 representations (9+10+11, 6+7+8+9, 4+5+6+7+8). 36 has odd factors 3,9 → 2 representations (11+12+13, 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8). 30 has more because it has more odd divisors. A wrong answer (e.g., "36 is bigger so more ways") reveals confusion between magnitude and divisor structure.

questions.q: A student claims: "All even numbers greater than 10 can be written as sums of consecutive numbers." Evaluate this claim and provide a counterexample if false.
questions.a: The claim is false. Counterexample: 16 (even, >10) cannot be expressed. Also 32, 64, etc. The student likely tested only a few numbers and generalized. A wrong evaluation (e.g., "true because 12,14,18 work") shows insufficient testing of powers of 2.

questions.q: Create an even number between 50 and 100 that has exactly three different representations as sums of consecutive natural numbers. Explain how you chose it.
questions.a: An even number with exactly three representations needs exactly four odd divisors (including 1). Example: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 (but <50). 2 × 3 × 7 = 42 (<50). 2 × 3 × 11 = 66 (odd divisors: 1,3,11,33 → 3 representations). 66 works: 21+22+23, 10+11+12+13+14+15, 1+2+...+11. A poor answer picks a random number without using odd divisor count.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: An even number can be expressed as a sum of two or more ______ natural numbers if and only if it is not a power of 2 (i.e., it has at least one odd factor greater than 1).
Fill in the blank: Imagine your class is arranging 24 ______ in a triangular formation where each row has one more chair than the row in front.
Fill in the blank: The number of ways to write an even number as such a sum equals the number of odd divisors of that number minus ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can determine whether a given even number can be written as a sum of consecutive natural numbers, find at least one such representation when possible, and explain why powers of 2 (like 2, 4, 8, 16, 32) are the only even numbers that cannot be expressed this way.
